files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.Core.Scheduler.IScheduler
files.Summary:
A scheduling policy: everything that decides which thread runs when. The mechanism around it (the thread registry, the lifecycle transitions, the timer-tick entry, the register save and restore) is fixed. Install an implementation with .

Every hook runs in the kernel's most sensitive window. Most are called with interrupts already masked, and the two scheduling hooks run inside the timer interrupt itself; each member below says which. No hook may block, park, or wait, and none may allocate on the tick path. Four get no mask from the manager (, and the two run-queue diagnostics) and must take themselves before touching the run structure. The spinlock around is not a substitute: it excludes another caller, not the tick.

Several hooks have no mechanism-side caller yet, because the kernel runs on one CPU and nothing in-tree sets priorities. Implement them, but do not expect them to be exercised.

Two rules hold for every hook. Each must tolerate being called more than once for the same thread, and each must tolerate an empty slot, because clears it and a thread can lose its record between a tick and the hook that observes it; that is why a hook reads the slot with as and never a cast. A record written by a different policy is never handed to a hook: re-homes every live thread through on the outgoing policy and on the incoming one.

Inspired by Ekiben's EkibenScheduler trait.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Diagnostics.KernelThreadInfo
files.Summary:
Point-in-time snapshot of one kernel thread, produced by . The snapshot is taken without locking the scheduler, so fields of a thread that is being rescheduled concurrently may be one tick stale.

This is a projection of , the thread control block on the experimental scheduler seam, and it is narrower on purpose. It carries what a monitor can render off an unlocked read: identity, state, and two totals. It leaves behind the saved stack pointer, the entry address, the stack base and the two scheduling timestamps, because each of those is meaningful only in a state the snapshot cannot guarantee it is observing, and a policy that wants them already holds the control block. Two names differ from the seam's, both to state a unit the seam leaves to its own docs: and .

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Diagnostics.Log
files.Summary: Kernel debug log, written to the platform serial port (COM1 on x64, PL011 on ARM64). This is the supported way for kernels to emit debug output that a host can capture; on QEMU the stream appears on the -serial device. Writes are synchronous, allocation-free for strings and numbers, and usable from the earliest phase of BeforeRun onward.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Diagnostics.MemoryInfo
files.Summary: Diagnostic view of the kernel's physical-memory and garbage-collector statistics, plus a forced collection. Every figure is a property, and each is a plain field read with no allocation, so they are safe to poll from a monitor loop at display refresh rate. The two collector counters are read independently rather than as a pair, so a collection landing between two reads shows up in one of them and not the other. Managed-heap figures beyond these counters come from the BCL ().

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Diagnostics.SchedulerInfo
files.Summary:
Diagnostic view of the kernel scheduler: feature and lifecycle state, per-CPU thread tables, and the global thread registry, plus a request to terminate a thread by ID. All reads are allocation-free and safe to poll from a monitor loop; snapshots of threads that are being rescheduled concurrently may be one tick stale.

Three shapes report "nothing there", and which one a member uses follows from what it is. A plain read answers with its own empty value, so , , , , and are 0 and is null before the scheduler exists, with no separate error channel. A read that must hand back a whole snapshot cannot express absence in the snapshot itself, so it is a Try and the bool carries that answer. is the one member that acts rather than reads, and a bool would not tell a caller which of five things happened, so it returns ; that enum is its failure channel as well, and it reports rather than throwing when the scheduler is compiled out.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Storage.Ebr
files.Summary:
EBR (Extended Boot Record) chain parser and editor. An extended partition contains a singly-linked list of EBR sectors; each EBR holds one logical partition entry plus an optional pointer to the next EBR. Convention used:

  • Logical-entry start LBA is relative to the EBR sector that holds it.
  • Next-EBR pointer is relative to the extended partition's start LBA (the standard convention).
  • The first EBR always sits at the extended partition's start LBA.
  • Each subsequent EBR is placed immediately after the prior logical's data.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Timer.AlarmManager
files.Summary:
Runs callbacks after a delay on a dedicated kernel thread. Alarm callbacks run in thread context, so they may block, allocate and use scheduler primitives, unlike the interrupt-context callbacks of . Requires the scheduler; resolution is bounded by the scheduler tick.

The scheduling calls themselves also run in thread context only. Every member here takes the alarm list's mutex and parks if it is held, so calling one from an interrupt handler, a callback included, parks inside the handler and hangs. The members mask interrupts instead of parking and have no such restriction.

Disposal is the one state the two halves of this interface report differently: every Try member answers false for a disposed handle, because that is what its bool already means, while and throw, having no count that means "the handle is gone" rather than "no bytes moved".

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Vfs.IVfsNodeHandle

The interface is disposable so both handle kinds work in using blocks, but only a file handle has anything to release: it owns the open-file state the driver keeps for a read or write position. Disposing a directory handle does nothing, and a directory handle stays usable afterwards.
